overview.title: Campaign Performance Overview
overview.subtitle: {count} campaigns analysed · AI accuracy ≥ 99.5% · Real-time revenue forecasting
overview.kpiRoiSub: revenue ÷ total budget · higher = more efficient spend
overview.salesDistributionSub: Number of campaigns by predicted revenue bracket
overview.correlationTip: Pearson r measures the linear relationship between a channel's budget and revenue across all campaigns. r=1.0 = perfect positive link; r=0 = no relationship. TV's high r means increasing TV spend reliably lifts revenue.
overview.efficiencyTip: Correlation-weighted revenue index: avg_revenue × Pearson_r for each channel. Shows which channel delivers the most revenue relative to the others. TV's high score means rebalancing budget toward TV is typically the highest-ROI move.
overview.benchmarksSub: Campaign tiers based on revenue percentile thresholds
overview.benchmarksTip: Campaigns are split into thirds by revenue: top 33% = High, middle 33% = Medium, bottom 33% = Low. The thresholds (Q33/Q66) are computed from the dataset and used by the classifier to label every campaign. Use these as your performance targets.
overview.tierHighDesc: Top 33% of campaigns — strong channel investment & tier engagement
overview.tierMediumDesc: Middle 33% — solid results with room to optimise channel mix
overview.tierLowDesc: Bottom 33% — underspend or misaligned channel weighting detected
overview.actionForecastSub: Predict sales from any budget mix in seconds
overview.actionOptimizerSub: Drag sliders — watch revenue react in real time
overview.actionPlannerSub: Set a revenue goal, get the optimal budget
overview.actionModelsSub: Inspect accuracy, R², RMSE and more
overview.noteSalesDistribution: Revenue is spread broadly across the $0–$360M range with no heavy clustering, indicating that the model was trained on campaigns spanning the full spectrum of marketing investment. The slight peaks at both ends reflect low-budget Nano campaigns and high-spend Mega campaigns, while the middle bands represent the majority of the training distribution.
overview.noteBudgetMix: TV represents ~{pct}% of the average total budget, confirming it as the dominant channel by spend. Radio and Social Media each absorb a smaller share. Since TV also shows the highest correlation with revenue (r = {tvCorr}), this allocation is well-optimised for revenue generation.
overview.noteInfluencer: Mega influencer campaigns generate the highest mean revenue, but this partly reflects that Mega campaigns also tend to have larger overall budgets — not just the influencer tier itself. Influencer tier is a low-importance feature in the model; budget magnitude (especially TV) is far more predictive of raw revenue.
overview.noteCorrelation: TV shows near-perfect linear correlation with revenue (r = {tvCorr}) — every dollar of TV spend maps almost directly to a predictable revenue lift. Radio is a strong secondary driver (r = {radioCorr}). Social Media has the weakest link (r = {smCorr}): at current spend levels, additional Social budget yields diminishing returns compared to an equivalent TV increase.
overview.noteEfficiency: The efficiency index weights each channel's average spend by its Pearson correlation with revenue. TV's dominant score means redirecting even a small fraction of Social Media budget toward TV typically generates a net positive return — use this as a reallocation guide.
overview.edaDividerSub: Statistical distributions, outlier detection & channel scatter analysis
overview.edaDistSub: 25-bin histograms across 4,572 campaigns · red = outlier zone · skewness and IQR shown per feature
overview.outlierSubIqr: Fences: Q1 − 1.5×IQR and Q3 + 1.5×IQR · coloured band = middle 50% · green tick = median
overview.scatterSubDashboard: 500 sampled campaigns · zero-budget rows excluded · coloured by influencer tier · Pearson r shown
overview.histNoteTv: TV budget spans $0–${max}M with a near-uniform distribution (skew ≈ {skew}). No significant outliers detected — campaigns are well-distributed across all budget levels, making TV the most stable predictor.
overview.histNoteRadio: Radio budget is also broadly distributed (mean ${mean}M, std ±${std}M). Its near-symmetric shape means the model sees balanced low-and-high Radio investment, supporting reliable correlation estimates with revenue.
overview.histNoteSocial: Social Media budget is compressed into a narrow range ($0–$50M), giving it less variance than TV or Radio. This limited spread partly explains Social Media's weaker correlation with revenue — the model has less signal to learn from at higher spend levels.
overview.histNoteSales: Revenue follows a broad, roughly uniform distribution from ${min}M to ${max}M. The balanced spread across the full range is ideal for regression — the model is exposed to all revenue levels rather than being biased toward a narrow band.
overview.summaryTableNote: All four features show near-zero skewness and zero IQR outliers, confirming a clean, well-bounded dataset. The IQR (Q3 − Q1) measures the central 50% spread — TV has the widest IQR ({tvIqr}M), reflecting the broadest range of investment. Sales IQR ({salesIqr}M) confirms that revenue is also widely distributed, giving the model a full range of outcomes to learn from.
overview.noOutliersExtended: No outliers detected in any feature using the IQR method. The dataset is clean and well-bounded across all channels — no campaign had an anomalously high or low budget for any channel relative to its peers. This means the model was not influenced by extreme data points during training.
overview.scatterTvNote: The TV-vs-Revenue scatter forms a nearly perfect straight line (r = {r}), confirming that TV spend is almost deterministically linked to campaign revenue. All four influencer tiers overlap closely, showing that TV spend dominates over tier choice for revenue prediction.
overview.scatterRadioNote: Radio shows a strong positive relationship with revenue (r = {r}), but with considerably more scatter than TV — indicating that Radio spend alone is less sufficient to predict revenue. The fan-shaped spread suggests Radio's effect is amplified when combined with TV investment.
overview.classPieNote: The three performance classes are exactly balanced by design — each contains ~{count} campaigns (~33%). This intentional balance ensures the classification models are trained without class-imbalance bias, giving equal predictive weight to High, Medium, and Low campaign outcomes.
overview.classHighCard: Top 33% revenue (> {q66}M) · Strong channel investment across TV and Radio
overview.classMediumCard: Middle 33% ({q33}M – {q66}M) · Solid results with room to optimise channel mix
overview.classLowCard: Bottom 33% (< {q33}M) · Underspend or misaligned channel weighting detected
overview.pairwiseNote: Budget channels (TV, Radio, Social Media) are nearly uncorrelated with each other (r ≈ 0), confirming no multicollinearity — each channel contributes independent, non-redundant signal to the regression model. TV × Sales and Radio × Sales show the strongest linear links, directly validating why these two channels dominate feature importance.

tips.r2: R-squared (coefficient of determination). Measures what fraction of revenue variance the model explains. 1.0 = perfect; 0.99 = explains 99% of variance. Higher is better.
tips.rmse: Root Mean Squared Error — the average prediction error in revenue units ($M). Penalises large errors more than MAE. Lower is better.
tips.mae: Mean Absolute Error — the average absolute difference between predicted and actual revenue ($M). More intuitive than RMSE; lower is better.
tips.cvR2: Cross-Validation R² — R² averaged over 5 folds of the training data (±std). Tests that the model generalises, not just memorises. High mean + low std = reliable model.
tips.accuracy: Fraction of campaigns correctly classified as High / Medium / Low performance. A score of 0.98 means 98% of predictions were correct.
tips.f1: F1-macro averages the F1 score across all classes (High/Medium/Low) equally, regardless of class size. Penalises models that ignore minority classes.
tips.roc: Area Under the ROC Curve — measures how well the model separates classes at any decision threshold. 1.0 = perfect; 0.5 = random. Higher is better.

predict.title: Revenue Forecast
predict.subtitle: Adjust budget sliders — the AI model predicts your revenue in real time
predict.purpose: I have a budget — what revenue will I get?
predict.inRangeTip: Budget is within the model's training data range. Predictions are reliable.
predict.extrapolatingTip: Budget exceeds the training range. The model is extrapolating — treat the prediction with caution.
predict.influencerMega: Mega: celebrity-scale reach, highest brand impact
predict.roiTip: Return on Investment: (Revenue ÷ Total Budget) × 100. A +150% ROI means every $1M spent generates $2.5M in revenue.
predict.efficiencyTip: Revenue multiplier: how many dollars of revenue are generated per $M of total marketing budget. 2.5× means $1M spent returns $2.5M.
predict.campaignClassTip: AI classification of this campaign as High / Medium / Low performance, based on the predicted revenue percentile. Confidence = fraction of classifier probability assigned to the predicted class.
predict.allModelsTip: Four ML models (Linear Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Neural Net) predict revenue independently. When they agree closely, the prediction is highly reliable. A wide spread signals the budget is in an uncertain region.
predict.allModelsSub: Model agreement signals prediction reliability. High spread = more uncertainty.

simulator.title: Budget Optimizer
simulator.subtitle: Drag sliders to rebalance your spend — revenue, ROI and sensitivity update live
simulator.purpose: I have a budget — how should I split it across channels?
simulator.revenueForecastTip: Predicted revenue from the best ML model (Random Forest) given your current budget mix.
simulator.roiTip: Return on Investment: (Predicted Revenue ÷ Total Budget) × 100. Positive % = profitable campaign at this budget level.
simulator.efficiencyTip: Revenue multiplier: dollars of revenue generated per $M of total budget. Drag sliders to find the allocation with the highest efficiency.
simulator.allModelsSub: Tight consensus = high prediction confidence. Wide spread = budget is near extrapolation boundaries.
simulator.tvSensitivityTip: Shows how predicted revenue changes as TV spend scales from $0 to maximum, with Radio and Social Media held at their current values. Useful for finding the point of diminishing returns on TV.
simulator.tvSensitivitySub: Revenue forecast as TV spend scales from 0 → {max}M · Radio={radio}M · SM={sm}M held fixed
simulator.trainingBoundaryTip: The dashed line marks the maximum TV spend seen during model training. Beyond this point the model is extrapolating — predictions become less reliable the further right you go.

targetPlanner.title: Target Planner
targetPlanner.subtitle: Two tools: find the budget to hit a revenue goal, or estimate your probability of hitting it
targetPlanner.purpose: I need $X revenue — what budget do I need, and can I hit it?
targetPlanner.inverseTip: Works backwards from a revenue target: gradient-based optimization iterates over TV/Radio/Social allocations until the model predicts a revenue meeting your goal, within the budget cap you set.
targetPlanner.inverseSub: Set a revenue target — the AI optimizer finds the TV / Radio / Social mix to reach it
targetPlanner.optError: Optimisation failed — verify the API server is running.
targetPlanner.notConvergedTip: Convergence means the optimizer found a budget allocation that exactly matches the target. Not converged means the algorithm stopped before reaching the exact target — often because the budget cap is too low. Raise the Max Budget Cap to allow more headroom.
targetPlanner.probabilityTip: Random Forest is an ensemble of 100+ decision trees. Each tree independently predicts revenue. The fraction of trees predicting ≥ your goal is the probability estimate — more reliable than a single model point estimate.
targetPlanner.probabilitySub: Given your budget, the Random Forest ensemble estimates P(revenue ≥ goal) using the spread of 100+ individual tree predictions
targetPlanner.probError: Analysis failed — Random Forest model may be unavailable.
targetPlanner.rfMeanTip: Average revenue predicted across all Random Forest trees. The ± std shows how spread out the individual tree predictions are — a low std means the ensemble is in strong agreement.
targetPlanner.treesTip: {n} individual decision trees vote on the outcome. More trees = smoother, more stable probability distribution.
targetPlanner.probGoalTip: Probability that your campaign revenue will meet or exceed the goal, estimated by the fraction of Random Forest trees predicting ≥ goal. ≥70% = high confidence · 40–70% = moderate · <40% = unlikely at this budget.
targetPlanner.distributionSub: Each bar = number of Random Forest trees predicting that revenue bracket. Green = above goal · Blue = below goal

insights.title: Revenue Drivers
insights.subtitle: Feature importance from {model} — what actually drives your revenue
insights.heroSub: {pct}% of model's decision weight · r = {r} correlation with revenue
insights.featureChartTip: Gini impurity reduction: each feature's score is how much it reduces uncertainty when splitting data across all trees. Higher = the model relies on this input more when predicting revenue. TV's high score confirms it's the primary revenue lever.
insights.featureChartSub: Impurity reduction across all decision trees
insights.channelCorrTip: Pearson r: the linear correlation between each channel's budget and revenue across 4,572 campaigns. r=0.9 means 90% of the variance in revenue can be explained by a straight-line relationship with that channel's spend.
insights.roiByInfluencerTip: Average revenue-to-budget ratio for campaigns grouped by influencer tier. A higher ROI means campaigns with that tier have historically generated more revenue per dollar spent. Note: influencer tier has low feature importance, so differences here may reflect spending patterns more than tier effectiveness.
insights.insightTvDesc: TV has the highest correlation with Sales (r={r}) and is the #1 feature by importance. Every $M of additional TV spend generates the strongest marginal revenue lift.
insights.insightRadioDesc: Radio shows r={r} — a strong secondary driver. Combined TV + Radio allocation explains the majority of campaign revenue variance.
insights.insightInfluencerDesc: Influencer dummy variables rank low in importance. Budget magnitude (especially TV) is far more predictive than influencer tier selection for raw revenue volume.
insights.insightSocialDesc: Social Media has the lowest correlation (r={r}) despite growing investment. Consider reallocating excess Social spend to TV for higher ROI.

analytics.title: Dataset Analytics
analytics.subtitle: {count} campaigns · Statistical distributions, outlier detection & pairwise correlations
analytics.kpiOutliersClean: No outliers detected across all features
analytics.distTip: Histograms show how each feature is distributed across all 4,572 campaigns. Red bars mark the outlier region (outside 1.5×IQR from Q1/Q3). Dashed blue = mean, dashed green = median.
analytics.distSub: 25-bin histograms · red = outlier region · blue dashed = mean · green dashed = median
analytics.summaryTip: Descriptive statistics for each numeric feature. IQR = interquartile range (Q3−Q1) — the spread of the middle 50% of data. Skewness > 1 or < −1 indicates a non-symmetric distribution. Outliers use the IQR method: values outside [Q1−1.5×IQR, Q3+1.5×IQR].
analytics.outlierTip: IQR method: a value is an outlier if it falls below Q1−1.5×IQR or above Q3+1.5×IQR. The shaded band shows the interquartile range (middle 50%). Green tick = median.
analytics.outlierSub: IQR fences: Q1 − 1.5×IQR and Q3 + 1.5×IQR · shaded band = middle 50% of data
analytics.noOutliersMsg: No outliers detected in any feature using the IQR method — the dataset is clean and well-bounded across all channels.
analytics.scatterTip: Scatter plots of budget vs revenue for the two strongest predictors, coloured by influencer tier. The Pearson r value in the top-right shows the linear correlation strength. A tight, rising cloud means budget reliably predicts revenue.
analytics.scatterSub: 500 sampled campaigns · coloured by influencer tier · Pearson r shown
analytics.infTip: Left: mean sales per tier with ±1 std error bars — shows the typical range around the average. Right: full box statistics (min, Q1, median, mean, Q3, max) — shows the distribution shape per tier.
analytics.infSub: Distribution of sales across Mega / Macro / Micro / Nano influencer tiers
analytics.classTip: Campaigns are split into thirds by revenue: top 33% = High, middle 33% = Medium, bottom 33% = Low. The thresholds are derived from the dataset quantiles and used by the classification models.
analytics.classSub: Balanced three-class split based on revenue quantiles (Q33 / Q66)
analytics.classMediumDesc: Middle 33% · solid results with room to optimise
analytics.classLowDesc: Bottom 33% · underspend or misaligned channel mix
analytics.corrTip: Pearson r between every pair of numeric features. Budget channels (TV, Radio, Social Media) are near-zero correlated with each other — no multicollinearity issue.

featureImportance.title: Feature Importance
featureImportance.subtitle: Understanding which inputs the model relies on · model: {model}
featureImportance.rankingTip: Each bar shows how much that feature reduces Gini impurity across all trees in the Random Forest. Gini impurity = uncertainty at a tree node. Higher reduction = the model splits on this feature more often = more influential on the final prediction.
featureImportance.rankingSub: Gini impurity reduction summed across all trees
featureImportance.correlationTip: Pearson r: a score from 0 to 1 measuring how strongly a channel's budget correlates with revenue. r > 0.7 = strong — every budget increase reliably lifts revenue. r < 0.4 = weak — other factors dominate.
featureImportance.corrStrong: Strong positive relationship — increasing spend directly lifts revenue
featureImportance.corrModerate: Moderate relationship — meaningful but not dominant driver
featureImportance.corrWeak: Weak relationship — diminishing returns at current investment levels
featureImportance.findingTvDesc: TV has the highest importance and r={r}. Increasing TV spend shows the strongest marginal return per dollar invested.
featureImportance.findingRadioDesc: Radio (r={r}) is a reliable secondary driver. TV + Radio together explain the bulk of revenue variance in the model.
featureImportance.findingInfluencerDesc: Influencer dummy variables rank low. Budget level (TV especially) is far more predictive than which influencer tier you choose for a campaign.
featureImportance.findingSocialDesc: Social Media shows r={r}. At current investment levels, additional Social spend yields lower revenue than an equivalent TV increase.
